what_it_does: When multiple graphics processors (GPUs) collaborate on a task, they share a large pool of memory, but moving data between a GPU's fast local memory and the slower shared pool is expensive. Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) is a software feature that tries to handle this automatically by moving pages (fixed-size chunks of data, typically 4 KB) between memories as needed — but it applies the same one-size-fits-all policy to all data regardless of how that data is actually used. OASIS watches how different data objects are accessed at runtime by tracking hardware counters that record how frequently each memory page is touched and in what pattern, then recognizes that the same object may be accessed in very different ways across different phases of a computation. Based on those observed patterns, it selects the best strategy per object per phase: immediately moving a page to the GPU that just touched it, migrating it more gradually based on access frequency, or duplicating it on multiple GPUs when several need the same data. This fine-grained, phase-aware approach improves overall system throughput without requiring programmers to manually manage memory placement.
